steps.body: Ordering a list uses the same spot-by-spot comparison — just check each pair of numbers the same way, one comparison at a time.

steps.body: Read a number, then use it.
explanationVariants: Hundreds word first, then the rest.

commonErrors.feedback: Don't drop the hundreds — two hundred is 200, plus sixteen is 216.
That's 4 digits. Two hundred sixteen is a 3-digit number: 216.

steps.body: To order a whole list, compare pairs one at a time, sliding the smaller or bigger one into place until the whole list is sorted.
Inspect one pair before sorting the whole set.

widget.prompt: Line up 267 and 627. Inspect the first place that decides their order.

choices.label: Hundreds place
choices.feedback: Yes. The hundreds are 2 and 6, so 267 must come before 627.

choices.label: Tens place
choices.feedback: Start with the hundreds, where 2 and 6 already differ.

choices.label: Ones place
choices.feedback: The ones do not speak first. Compare the hundreds before moving right.

widget.successFeedback: The hundreds decide: 2 hundreds is less than 6 hundreds, so 267 comes before 627.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open the hundreds stage before choosing the deciding place.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Compare from left to right. The first difference is 2 hundreds versus 6 hundreds.

predict.prompt: 267 and 627 use the same digits in different places. Which place should you compare first?
predict.reveal: The aligned chart opens at the hundreds: 2 hundreds versus 6 hundreds. That first difference puts 267 before 627.

steps.body: Order a whole set at once — same digits, different spots.

widget.prompt: Drag the four numbers into order, least to greatest. Every one uses only the digits 2, 6, and 7.

misorderFeedback.feedback: 627 has 6 hundreds; 276 has only 2. Hundreds are checked first, and 2 hundreds loses to 6 no matter how the other digits look.
Both start with 2 hundreds, so the TENS decide: 267 carries 6 tens, 276 carries 7 — so 267 comes first.
Both hold 6 hundreds — the tens break the tie: 2 tens (627) sits before 7 tens (672).

widget.missFeedback: Sort by hundreds first (the 2-hundreds pair before the 6-hundreds pair), then let tens order each pair: 267, 276, 627, 672.
widget.successFeedback: 267 < 276 < 627 < 672 — hundreds split the pairs, tens ordered within. Same digits, four different sizes.

steps.body: Write and compare go hand in hand — a story might give you a number in words, and you'll need to compare it against another number.
Write a word-form number, mixed practice.

options.label: seven hundred thirty
options.feedback: Yes — 7 hundreds, then thirty (0 ones, not spoken).

options.label: seven hundred three
options.feedback: 730 has 3 tens and 0 ones — that's "thirty," not "three."

options.label: seventy-three
options.feedback: Don't drop the hundreds: seven hundred thirty, not seventy-three.

steps.body: A comparison with the ones spot deciding.
explanationVariants: Hundreds and tens match; ones decide: 6 < 9, so 456 < 459.
The ones spot breaks the tie.

options.feedback: Yes — hundreds (4=4) and tens (5=5) match, so ones decide: 6 < 9, meaning 456 < 459.
Hundreds and tens are tied. Check the ones: 6 < 9, so 456 < 459, not >.
Hundreds and tens match, but the ones differ (6 vs 9) — not equal.

commonErrors.feedback: "Eight hundred" means 8 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones: 800, not just 8.

explanationVariants: Check spot by spot until you find a difference.

hints: Compare the hundreds digit first: 7 = 7, tied.
Move to the tens digit: 9 vs 2.

steps.body: Ordering a list just repeats spot-by-spot comparison for every pair — reading and writing numbers helps along the way.
takeaways: Order a list by comparing pairs, spot by spot.
Word form and standard form both describe the same number.
The same left-to-right comparison strategy works for any pair.

concept.body: Ordering numbers uses the same spot-by-spot comparison as before: hundreds, then tens, then ones. Reading and writing word form helps interpret story problems along the way.
